source: Kim, Yang, Min, Jung (2026) Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency (ReASC)
finding: A two-stage method. Stage 1 accepts a single sample if its token-confidence is high enough (a threshold calibrated on 128 held-out items for 90% target accuracy). Accepted single answers were very accurate. Confidence is a usable gate for 'the first answer is safe'.
numbers: Offline accepted share and accuracy of accepted answers: GSM8K 49-61% of items accepted at 91.3-98.6% accuracy; MATH500 7-38% accepted at 86.1-97.3% (LLaMA-3.2-3B, Gemma-3-4B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-3-27B). Online calibration, LLaMA-3B GSM8K: 28.1% accepted at 93.5%. Cost cut up to 70% vs self-consistency k=16 at similar accuracy (GSM8K Gemma-3-4B). Qwen2.5-7B accuracy by confidence quintile: 20.0, 40.2, 51.9, 82.9, 93.3%. AUROC of Bottom-10%-group confidence 0.860 vs plain self-certainty 0.801.
limits: Math and a few QA sets only (GSM8K, MATH500, Omni-Math, GPQA-Diamond); open 3B-27B models; needs held-out labels or an unlabeled mixture-model calibration; threshold must be recalibrated per model and task. Share accepted falls sharply on harder sets.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2: token confidence of the first sample (bottom 10% group confidence) can replace 'years of experience' as the recognition gate, if calibrated per task class on a small labeled set.

source: Aghazadeh, Ghasemi, Beyhaghi, Pishro-Nik (2026) CGES: Confidence-Guided Early Stopping for Self-Consistency
finding: Bayesian early stopping from per-answer confidence cuts calls by more than half with almost no accuracy loss, but the confidence signal fails on GPQA, so the gate is not universal.
numbers: Budget 16: average calls 16.0 to 6.7-7.5 (58% fewer) within 0.2 pp of self-consistency on every set except GPQA; most efficient variant 6.71 calls at -0.4 pp. Five sets: AIME24 (30 problems), MATH500, GSM8K, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro. Qwen2.5-7B for most; R1-Distill-Qwen-7B for AIME24 and GPQA.
limits: Weak where the confidence signal is uninformative (GPQA); proofs assume calibrated or drift-condition confidence; small open models; a missing right answer among candidates cannot be recovered.
agent_relevance: Supports a per-task-class validity check on the fast path (K23): disable recognise-first where confidence does not separate right from wrong, as on GPQA.

source: Saparkhan, Hawasly, Parvez, Raza (2026) Self-Consistency from Only Two Samples: CoT-PoT Ensembling
finding: Agreement between a chain-of-thought answer and an executed-program answer is a very strong sign the answer is safe. Stopping at the first cross-modal agreement solved most items with two samples and beat full self-consistency.
numbers: 78.6% of items solved with two samples on average; sample count cut 9.3x (best prior early-stopping 5.6x); the most efficient variant (CPAA) had 0.8% higher accuracy than full CoT self-consistency. P(safe | agreement) estimated near 1 on all five models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, Mistral-Large, Qwen3-Coder, DeepSeek-R1). 500 test cases from each of GSM8K, MATH, FinQA, SVAMP, TabMWP; max 40 samples.
limits: Numeric-answer tasks where a program can be written; agreement is cheap only when two modalities exist; priors estimated from 100 held-out items per dataset.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 and gap 4: a two-route agreement check (reasoning vs executable check) is a cheap gate and a partly sound check. Likely transfers to code and arithmetic items, not open-ended ones.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: The best use of extra tokens depends on question difficulty. On easy questions more search against a verifier can hurt, and sequential revision works best. On hard ones, search beats best-of-N. A difficulty-adaptive policy was over 4x more efficient than best-of-N.
numbers: MATH, PaLM-2 variants. Difficulty = five quantiles of the model's own pass@1 from 2048 samples (oracle) or from verifier scores (predicted); both curves nearly overlap. Easy bins 1-2: beam search degrades as budget rises (4 to 256 generations) while best-of-N does not; bins 3-4: beam search beats best-of-N; bin 5: no method progresses. Best-of-N matched with up to 4x less compute. Easy questions best with fully sequential compute at budget 128.
limits: One model family, math only, process reward model verifier; difficulty estimate costs samples; no direct test of one candidate plus short check against a token-matched majority vote.
agent_relevance: Closest answer to gap 1: at equal compute, 'one answer then revise' wins on easy items and breadth wins on hard items. A gate on estimated difficulty is the real design variable.

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Real-environment best-first search with a model value function beats a compute-matched best-of-n re-ranking. The quality of the value function (the check) limits the gain, and depth plus breadth both help up to depth 5.
numbers: VisualWebArena 200-task subset, GPT-4o. No search 24.5%; search budget c=20 37.0% (+51% relative). Re-ranking baseline plateaus near 30% at about 7 runs; search at c=5 uses about equal compute and beats it. Value function ablation: none 24.5; LLaVA (n=20 consistency) 30.0; GPT-4o no consistency 28.5; GPT-4o n=5 32.5; n=20 37.0; ground-truth reward 43.5. Headline: 26.4% on full VWA (+39.7%), 19.2% on WebArena (+28.0%).
limits: Search acts in the real environment (backtracking is costly), not in imagination. Table 3 depth and breadth rows were hard to parse from the text; direction (more tree, more success up to d=5, b=5) is clear.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 3: check quality explains a large share of the gain (24.5 to 43.5 as the value signal improves); depth up to 5 helped here, unlike MENSA, so best depth is task and check dependent.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?
finding: With the same generator, replacing an LLM critic with a sound external verifier lifted Blocksworld plan accuracy from 55% to 88%. The LLM critic gave many false positives.
numbers: GPT-4, 100 random Blocksworld instances: generator only 40/100; LLM+LLM with back-prompting 55/100; LLM+VAL (sound verifier) with back-prompting 88/100. Binary vs detailed feedback made little difference.
limits: One domain, one model, n=100, no token matching beyond iteration caps.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: most of the gain of check-and-revise comes from check soundness, not from the act of simulating. Use code execution or constraint checkers as the check where they exist.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Across the literature, no prior work shows successful self-correction using feedback from a prompted LLM, except on tasks exceptionally suited to it. Self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists, and with large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Survey, no pooled effect size. Checklist for fair experiments given.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Survey of papers, mostly 2022-2024; I read the abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: do not rely on prompted self-simulation as a check; wire in executable or rule-based checks.

source: Chen, Li, Cakir, Akcali, Lee, Mattar (2026) Extracting Search Trees from LLM Reasoning Traces Reveals Myopic Planning
finding: In four-in-a-row, LLM reasoning models search shallowly (about 2 plies), and win-rate is predicted by how many first moves they consider, not by depth. Move choice is explained by a model that ignores deep nodes. This is the opposite of human experts, whose strength tracks depth.
numbers: 27 models, 4 games per pair, 1404 games; 14 models with full traces: 9696 traces, 1092 games. Mean max depth 1.78 +/- 0.71 plies (range 1.00-3.48) vs human estimates 4-6. Regression on win rate: depth beta=-0.015, p=0.82; breadth beta=0.075, p=0.0025. Pruning CoT paragraphs: move changes track shallow nodes, not deep ones (read at summary level).
limits: Board game; traces parsed by an LLM judge (GPT-5), so tree extraction has noise; correlational across models plus a pruning check.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for our model class, extra depth is not where the gain comes from; breadth of candidates is. Cap rollouts at about 2-3 steps and spend tokens on alternatives and a sound check.

source: Kuperwajs, Russek, Schut, Sagiv, Mattar, Ma, Griffiths (2025) Exploring resource-rational planning under time pressure in online chess (CogSci 2025 proceedings, pp. 3877-3883)
finding: In a fixed online chess position where extra search changes nothing (low value of computation), move quality did not depend on thinking time. In a position where deeper search finds a better move (high value), quality rose with time up to a plateau, and weaker players gained most; strong players already played well at the fastest control.
numbers: Lichess games 2022-2023; Stockfish depth 1 vs depth 15 defines value of computation (VOC). Low-VOC position: 12,384 moves; high-VOC position (VOC about 0.15 win probability): 12,786 moves; 9 time controls (60+0 to 900+10). Move entropy did not fall with more time. Elo 20th vs 80th percentile split.
limits: Observational, one position per VOC class, Stockfish as truth; players chose their own time control.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the safe-first-answer gate can be 'does a deeper look change the answer?'. Probe it with a cheap second look; skip rollouts where depth 1 and depth k agree.

source: Mei, Guo, Chang, Dong, Lee, Niu, Jiang (2026) R-WoM: Retrieval-augmented World Model for Computer-use Agents (ICLR 2026)
finding: LLMs identify the true next state well (above 75%) but their full-procedure plans rarely align with reference procedures (65% at best). Adding retrieved tutorials lifted plan alignment sharply, and the end-to-end agent gained, most on longer horizons.
numbers: Probe table (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B / Claude-3.5-Sonnet / Claude-3.7-Sonnet): next-state identification 77.0 / 81.0 / 86.0; plan alignment without retrieval 50 / 55 / 65, with retrieval 90 / 85 / 95; milestone recognition 83.7 / 85.7 / 86.7. Plan-alignment probe is small (steps of 20-multiples suggest about 20 tasks; not confirmed). End-to-end relative gains over the strongest non-R-WoM baseline: OSWorld +21.5 / +10.8 / +23.4%, WebArena +16.3 / +8.0 / +5.6%.
limits: Judge is an LLM (Claude-3.7-Sonnet); small probe samples; tutorials exist only for some tasks (276 OSWorld tasks lack references).
agent_relevance: Gap 10: retrieval grounding closes much of the long-horizon gap in this setting, but only where a tutorial or reference exists; where it does not, expect rollouts to stop helping after a few steps.

source: Li et al. (2026) Bridging the Agent-World Gap: Text World Models for LLM-based Agents (survey)
finding: A survey that restates that single-step state prediction saturates on structured text environments but collapses over multi-step rollouts, and that accuracy and downstream usefulness can come apart.
numbers: Reported secondhand: full-state prediction single-step accuracy 99% on ALFWorld and SciWorld; LLMs over 75% on next-state identification but rarely over 65% on full-procedure planning alignment (R-WoM); Task2Quiz finds task success and environment understanding dissociate.
limits: Secondary survey; I did not open the cited primary papers except R-WoM (d10). Numbers are as the survey reports them.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: ceiling depends on environment type. Structured, code-like state is simulated well; open-ended web or social state is not. Prefer executable simulators where possible.

source: Kim, Kim, Park et al. (2026) InvThink: Premortem Reasoning for Safer Language Models
finding: A prompt that first lists how the answer could go wrong, then answers under constraints, cut judged harm more than a plain safety instruction at similar token counts. A forward-direction control trained the same way was indistinguishable, so the gain may come from structure, not from the inverse direction.
numbers: TRIDENT professional-ethics tasks: judged harmfulness 3.22 (zero-shot) to 2.19 (InvThink prompt), -32%; SafetyPrompt 2.62 at similar token counts. Insider-threat scenarios: blackmail -90%, attempted murder -44% on average. Controlled SFT (23,063 targets, Qwen-2.5-7B): PROTHINK forward corpus vs InvThink harmfulness 1.01 vs 1.23, both safety rate 1.000, attack success 0.000.
limits: Safety and refusal behaviour, not decision accuracy. Judged by LLMs. The control null is at SFT only, on refusal-style data. No token-matched neutral prompt in the prompt-only comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: partial. A failure-enumeration step beats a bare instruction, but there is no evidence yet that it beats a length-matched neutral step on task accuracy.

source: Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989) Back to the future: Temporal perspective in the explanation of events
finding: The paper that introduced prospective hindsight, read from its abstract page only. Its stated results: in experiment 1, temporal perspective (future vs past framing) had little effect, while outcome certainty changed the explanations (longer, more episodic, past tense). Experiment 2: uncertainty changes the type of explanation, not time spent.
numbers: A search snippet (not the paper) gives experiment 1 as 114 MBA students; the often-quoted '30% more reasons' figure does not appear in the abstract text I read.
limits: Abstract only, via an index page; full text not opened. This conflicts with the common retelling that imagining the outcome as already happened gives a clean 30% boost. No decision-quality outcome measure in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the premortem has weak primary support. Treat a counter-cue step as a hypothesis to test at equal tokens, not as a proven human-validated operator.

source: Klein (2007) Performing a Project Premortem (Harvard Business Review)
finding: The fetched page text (probably a public summary) gives the premortem method and the claim that it makes dissent safe, but contains no controlled test, no Mitchell citation and no 30% figure.
limits: Likely only a summary of a paywalled article; absence of a citation here does not prove absence in the full article.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: no human outcome data on premortem effects on decision quality was found in this pass.

source: Ouyang, Yan, Hsu et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Memory of distilled strategies (from both successes and failures) beat memory of raw trajectories and memory of success-only workflows on WebArena.
numbers: WebArena 684 tasks, Gemini-2.5-flash, overall success: no memory 40.5; Synapse (trajectories) 42.1; AWM (workflows) 44.1; ReasoningBank 48.8; with parallel scaling (MaTTS) 51.8. Average steps 9.7 / 9.2 / 9.0 / 8.3 / 7.9. Gains over no memory +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 across three backbones.
limits: Confounded: ReasoningBank also uses failures and an LLM judge for success labels, so the abstraction level is not isolated. Not a clean prototype-versus-exemplar test.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: partial support for strategy-level (prototype-like) memory over raw cases. A clean ablation with the same content at two abstraction levels is still missing.

source: Calderwood, Klein, Crandall (1988) Time pressure, skill, and move quality in chess (Am J Psychol 101, 481-493); Klein, Wolf, Militello, Zsambok (1995) Characteristics of skilled option generation in chess (OBHDP)
finding: Not retrieved. Searches returned only citation details. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited, the publisher page returned 403, and the Springer page that cites the 1988 study redirected to a login. No figures were read.
numbers: None. Do not cite any number from these studies.
limits: Only citation details seen (the 1988 study is cited by van Harreveld et al. 2007), not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Needs a library copy or the Klein book chapters.
